podcast.title: Admiration for Bob Wills' Music (1938)
podcast.body: In 1938, Les Paul, already a famous guitarist, traveled from Waukesha, Wisconsin, to Tulsa, Oklahoma, specifically to hear Bob Wills' band play after his mother introduced him to Wills' music on the radio. This demonstrates the mutual respect that existed between musicians across genre and racial lines. "Paul was so amazed by Bob Willes' music that in 1938 he traveled from Waukesha, Wisconsin, where he was visiting his mother, to Tulsa, Oklahoma, to hear Willes' band play."

podcast.title: Collaboration with Gibson (1952)
podcast.body: Gibson approached Les Paul, a guitarist and inventor who was having a string of hits, to put his name on a new guitar model to boost sales. Paul agreed to the collaboration. "Would he allow Gibson to put his name on a new guitar to help sell it? What do you think? This agreed."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Story of the Electric Guitar - Part 2

podcast.title: Name Transfer to SG Design (1961)
podcast.body: In 1961, Les Paul transferred his name to Gibson's new solid body design, the SG, for a couple of years until his contract with the company expired. "In 1961, Les Paul transferred his name to a new solid body design called the SG for a couple of years until his contract with the company ran out."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Story of the Electric Guitar - Part 2

podcast.title: Collaboration with Gibson
podcast.body: Despite approaching multiple manufacturers with his ideas for guitar design, only Gibson expressed interest, leading to the creation of the iconic guitar that bears his name. "Les Paul took his ideas to a couple of different manufacturers, but only Gibson seemed interested."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Story of the Electric Guitar - Part 1

podcast.title: Consultant for Gibson
podcast.body: Paul had been actively "pestering" Gibson since the mid-1940s about developing a new type of electric guitar. The company eventually brought him in-house to work as a consultant alongside Gibson designer Tim McCarty. "Paul had been pestering Gibson about such things since the mid-1940s. The company finally said, OK, all right, fine. Let's see what you can do."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Rock's Most Iconic Instruments

podcast.title: Early Tinkering and Home Studio
podcast.body: Les Paul was a country and jazz guitarist and an inventor who established one of the very first home studios. Throughout the 1920s and late 1930s, he experimented with acoustic guitar designs. "He was a country and jazz guitarist and also an inventor who was among the very first musicians to have a home studio. Through the 20s and late 30s, he started tinkering with guitar design, acoustic guitars."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Story of the Electric Guitar - Part 1

podcast.title: Electric Guitar Pioneer – Clean Sound (1950s)
podcast.body: Les Paul was one of the most famous figures who contributed to the birth of the electric guitar in the 1950s. The initial objective for this instrument was to achieve volume with clean, clear, and amplified guitar sounds, focusing on fidelity rather than distortion. "Alright, that's Les Paul back in the 1950s doing his jazz thing on one of his electric guitar creations."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Inventors

podcast.title: Experimentation with Music Technology
podcast.body: Les Paul was a jazz and pop artist known for his pioneering experiments in creating his own electric guitars and his work with early multi-track tape machine technology. His innovations were fundamental to the development of modern recording. "He was a jazz and pop artist who experimented with making his own electric guitars, as well as messing around with this new multi-track tape machine technology."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Full Endorsement of His Signature Guitar
podcast.body: After working with Gibson on various shapes, designs, and materials for approximately a year, Les Paul was so pleased with the final product that he gave it his full, enthusiastic endorsement. In recognition, Gibson named the iconic guitar after him. "Les Paul loved the final product so much that he gave it a full-throated endorsement. And Gibson returned the favor by naming the guitar after him."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Rock's Most Iconic Instruments

podcast.title: Influence of Charlie Christian on Electric Guitar Design
podcast.body: In 1939, likely inspired by hearing Charlie Christian play, Les Paul conceived his own design for an electric guitar, which he dubbed "the log." This marked a significant shift in his focus towards electrification. "But in 1939, most likely after hearing Charlie Christian, he came up with an idea for his own electric guitar design."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Story of the Electric Guitar - Part 1

podcast.title: Influenced by Gene Autry
podcast.body: Les Paul was among the musicians significantly influenced by Gene Autry, who held the status of the biggest Western music star in the late 1930s and early 1940s. "influenced everyone from Les Paul to Bowie Didley."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 45: "Blueberry Hill", by Fats Domino

podcast.title: Invention of Sound-on-Sound Recording
podcast.body: Les Paul is credited with inventing Sound on Sound Recording, now commonly known as multitrack recording, which he developed in his garage home studio. This innovation significantly influenced future recording techniques. "Les Paul went on to invent Sound on Sound Recording, which is what we now call Multitrack Recording. He came up with that in the home studio in his garage."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Story of the Electric Guitar - Part 1

podcast.title: Meeting Charlie Christian
podcast.body: While jamming with Bob Wills' band in Oklahoma in 1938, Les Paul met Charlie Christian, a Black guitarist, during an interval. Paul was impressed by Christian's skill and invited him to join the jam, marking their first encounter shortly before Christian received an offer from Benny Goodman. "That was the first time that Les Paul met his friend Charlie Christian, shortly before Christian got the offer from Benny Goodman, hanging out and jamming at a Bob Willes gig."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 3: "Ida Red" by Bob Wills and the Texas Playboys

podcast.title: Multi-Track Recording Innovation
podcast.body: Les Paul was given an early production unit of the reel-to-reel tape machine by Ampex and subsequently modified it to allow for multi-track recording. This groundbreaking innovation made overdubs possible, meaning entire parts of a recording could be redone without having to re-record all other parts. It also facilitated the addition of special effects like reverb and echo after the fact and allowed for separate control of the volume of each track. "An early production unit was given to guitarist Les Paul, who modified the machines to allow for multi-track recording."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Unsung Heroes of Music: Part 1

podcast.title: Overdubbing Pioneer (1940s)
podcast.body: Guitarist and tinkerer Les Paul was instrumental in developing the technique of overdubbing. Working with the Ampex 200 reel-to-reel tape recorder, he made it possible to record new parts onto previously made recordings, fundamentally changing music production by allowing artists to improve on reality and create recordings that could not be performed live. "thanks to the work of guitarist and tinker rear less Paul, it was possible to overdub parts on previously made recordings."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Connections

podcast.title: Piano Collaboration with Nat King Cole
podcast.body: Nat King Cole played piano alongside Les Paul and Illinois Jacquet, demonstrating the collaborative environment of musicians in that era. "We've heard Nat King Cold before, playing piano with Les Paul and Illinois Jocquette..."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 32: "I Got A Woman" by Ray Charles

podcast.title: Pioneer of Overdubbing (Late 1940s)
podcast.body: Les Paul was a pioneer of overdubbing techniques in the late 1940s, and his sophisticated methods were later crudely emulated by Norman Petty. "Petty was a former musician who had performed crude experiments in overdubbing in the late 40s, copying Les Paul and Mary Ford, though in a much less sophisticated manner."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode Sixty-One: "That'll Be the Day", by the Crickets

podcast.title: Pioneering Sound-on-Sound Recording
podcast.body: Les Paul, a guitarist, began experimenting with his tape machine to create innovative recordings. He developed a technique to make "sound on sound" recordings by playing a song, rewinding the tape, and then recording another part over what was already laid down. He repeated this process multiple times to create the illusion of a large ensemble of guitarists, even though he was the only performer. "He figured out a way to make sound on sound recordings."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The More Things Change Part 2

podcast.title: Public Reception and Realization of Solid-Body Potential
podcast.body: Although "the log" was often mocked for its unusual appearance, its solid-body design led to the realization that guitars could adopt any shape. This opened new possibilities for guitar manufacturing. "People really made fun of the way the log looked. At the same time, they realized that by making a guitar with a solid body, a guitar could basically assume any shape you wanted. That had potential."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Story of the Electric Guitar - Part 1

podcast.title: Purist Backlash Against Overdubbing
podcast.body: Les Paul's sound-on-sound recordings, an early form of overdubbing, drew extreme criticism from purists who viewed it as "cheating." They argued that this music deceived the listener because it was impossible for one man to perform it live, deeming it "wrong, wrong, wrong." This fierce opposition contributed to the American Federation of Musicians issuing an edict against overdubbing. "The purists were apoplectic. That's even worse cheating. This music deceives the listener. It's impossible for one man to play this live, so it is wrong, wrong, wrong."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The More Things Change Part 2

podcast.title: The Log Guitar Design
podcast.body: "The log" was a rudimentary solid-body electric guitar constructed from a 4x4 piece of pine, to which two wings were attached to mimic the appearance of a Spanish guitar. It featured a regular guitar neck, a bridge, and two crude homemade pickups, making it distinct from the hollow-body electric guitars available at the time. "The result was something he called the log. It was a 4x4 piece of pine with two wings attached to it to make it look like a Spanish guitar. He attached a regular guitar neck to that body, along with a bridge and two crude homemade pickups. Unlike all the other electric guitars in the market, this one wasn't hollow. Its body was solid."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Story of the Electric Guitar - Part 1

podcast.title: The Log's Recording and Companion Instrument
podcast.body: A recording made in 1948 features "the log" along with another experimental instrument called "the Clunker." The Clunker was an old hollow-body guitar modified with a hole in the back, allowing Les Paul to easily access and "lobotomize" its internal electronics, effectively making it a playable workbench. "OK, that's not exactly Jimmy Hendrix, but again, that recording was made in 1948. We hear the log on that track, along with another monster called the Clunker, which was an old hollow body with a hole in the back that allowed Les Paul to lobotomize all the electronics inside. It was like a workbench you could play."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Story of the Electric Guitar - Part 1

podcast.title: Unveiling of the Gibson Les Paul Guitar
podcast.body: The first Gibson Les Paul guitar was officially unveiled on June 24, 1952, during a special event hosted for musicians at the Waldorf Astoria Hotel in New York. This landmark guitar was crafted from mahogany and featured a distinctive bright gold finish. "The first Gibson Les Paul was unveiled on June 24, 1952, at a special event for musicians at the Waldorf Astoria Hotel in New York."

xref.title: Guitar Sale to Adam Slack
xref.body: Mike McCready sold a full-size Les Paul guitar to Adam Slack of The Struts, an instrument Slack considers his best due to its exceptional tuning stability. "He also has a full-size Les Paul that he bought from Mike McCready of Pearl Jam."

srcs.episode: Modern Guitar Heroes:  The Men

xref.title: Impact on Modern Recording Techniques
xref.body: Along with investor Bing Crosby and guitarist Les Paul, Jack Mullin is credited with giving birth to modern recording studio techniques from the 1950s onward. His work with reel-to-reel tape made it possible for performances to be started, stopped, restarted, and edited with a razor blade and tape. Mistakes could be excised, jokes cut out, and overdubs became possible, allowing parts of a recording to be redone without affecting others. This also enabled the separate control of track volumes and the post-production addition of special effects like reverb and echo, transforming the studio into a musical instrument. "In short, Major Jack Moan, along with his early believer Bing Crosby and guitarist Les Paul, gave birth to modern recording studio techniques."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Unsung Heroes of Music: Part 1

xref.title: James E. High's Guitar Preference Evolution
xref.body: James E. High initially played a Teisco K2L, but later became a significant enthusiast of Gibson guitars, including various Les Paul models, a Flying V, and a 1991 special edition SG. "James E. High is playing a Tesco K2L, which is different for him because he became a big fan of Gibson guitars, including a variety of Les Paul's, a flying V, and a special edition SG from 1991."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Story of the Electric Guitar - Part 1

xref.title: Kevin Parker's Vox AC30 Setup
xref.body: Kevin Parker of Tame Impala employs a Vox AC30 amplifier in conjunction with unusual combinations of effects pedals and various guitars, including Fender Stratz, a Rickenbacker 335, and an Epiphone Les Paul model. While studio processing can obscure his exact live sound, his Vox AC30 is reliably used for performances. "It's hard to tell exactly what he's playing through on this track because of all the studio processing, but it's a good bet that when he plays it live, it's his Vox AC30 providing the noise."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Story of the Electric Guitar - Part 3

xref.title: Les Paul Custom on "While My Guitar Gently Weeps"
xref.body: George Harrison notably played a Gibson Les Paul Custom during the recording of "While My Guitar Gently Weeps." This demonstrates the versatility of the Les Paul model across different musical contexts and artists. "Now keep in mind that this is the same type of guitar George Harrison plays on while my guitar gently weeps."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Rock's Most Iconic Instruments

xref.title: Les Paul Jr. and Reggae Sound
xref.body: Bob Marley was a notable fan of Gibson's Les Paul guitars, particularly the Les Paul Jr., which he modified. The unique sound produced by this instrument, tailored to his specifications, played a crucial role in bringing reggae music to a global audience. "Bob Marley was a fan of the Les Paul guitars Gibson eventually started making. His main instrument was a Gibson Les Paul Jr. He modified it a bit, and the sound it produced brought reggae to the world."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Story of the Electric Guitar - Part 1

xref.title: Musical Style and Equipment
xref.body: Embrace's musical style featured loud guitars, prioritizing strumming over complex riffing. Their preferred equipment included Gips, Les Paul, or SG guitars, which were played through Marshall Tube amps, with a strict rule against using transistor amplifiers. "The guitars were loud, but there was less riffing and more strumming. Favorite guitars were Gips and Les Paul's or SG's, played through Marshall Tube amps. No transistors allowed."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Alt Rock Revivals Part 3: Emo

xref.title: Overdubbed Les Paul Sound
xref.body: In 1977, Steve Jones of the Sex Pistols achieved a thick, heavy sound by overdubbing his Gibson Les Paul Custom approximately 20 times. This technique showcased the guitar's capability for aggressive tones in punk rock. "He's playing a Gibson Les Paul custom that has been overdubbed unto itself around 20 times to get that thick, heavy sound."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Rock's Most Iconic Instruments

xref.title: Reliable Les Paul from Mike McCready
xref.body: He owns a full-size Les Paul that he purchased from Mike McCready of Pearl Jam, which he regards as his best instrument due to its consistent ability to stay in tune. "He actually calls this the best instrument he's ever owned because it never seems to go out of tune."
